Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 76
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Mechanic
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Earth/Outdoor): Soil or outdoor smells, Stress: Stress, Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Vignette:
Mai Tran was seventy-six years old and had been a mechanic since she immigrated to the United States in her twenties. She worked out of a small garage attached to her home in a quiet suburban neighborhood, and for decades her hands had known the weight of wrenches and the grit of engine grease. The stalking began about eighteen months ago, though at first she did not recognize it as such. A man in a dark sedan had started parking at the far end of her street, then moving closer each week. She noticed him first when she was weeding the flowerbed near her mailbox. He sat watching, engine idling, and she smelled the damp earth from the freshly turned soil as she straightened to look at him. That smell—rich, mineral, the particular scent of the ground after a light rain—became seared into the moment, and now any whiff of outdoor earth could send her heart racing.

The stalking escalated over several weeks. He began leaving small items on her front step: a dirty glove, a scrap of paper with her name written in block letters, a handful of soil. Mai called the police twice, but he was never there when they arrived, and without a clear threat they could do little. Her husband, a retired electrician, wanted to confront the man, but Mai insisted they do nothing, certain it would make things worse. The worst moment came one evening when she returned from the grocery store and found him standing in her driveway, just staring. She froze. The paper bag slipped from her arms, and the man turned and walked away without a word. That image—his silhouette against the garage light, the way he moved so slowly—stayed with her like a photograph she could not put down. When she tries to tell anyone about it now, she loses the thread. Her mouth opens, but the words scatter, and she ends up staring at the floor. She has learned to stop mid-sentence because the effort to finish feels like wading through mud, and she would rather push the entire memory away before it fully arrives.

In the months that followed, Mai’s life narrowed. She stopped gardening entirely, though it had been her quiet joy. The smell of soil reached her even when she was inside—if her husband came in from digging in his vegetable patch, she would catch the scent on his clothes and feel a clammy dread. She found herself scanning her rearview mirror constantly while driving to the auto parts store, and at the garage she would catch herself looking over her shoulder toward the driveway every few minutes. Even inside her own home, sitting in her armchair, she felt watched. The walls did not feel like protection; they felt like a stage. She began leaving the kitchen lights on all night, and she would not sit with her back to a window.

Her work suffered in ways that were hard to name. She had always been meticulous, but now she would stop in the middle of replacing a brake line to check that nobody had walked up behind her. Customers noticed her short replies, the way she kept one eye on the door. Her husband began to worry when she flinched at the sound of his key in the lock. She could not tolerate feeling happy or relaxed; a few minutes of ease would dissolve into a vague sense of danger, as if her own contentment was a signal to whatever had been after her. Stress, too, was a trigger—the pressure of a difficult repair or a tight deadline would flood her with the same helpless alertness she had felt in the driveway.

What finally brought Mai to seek help was a morning last month when she could not bring herself to open the garage door. She stood in the kitchen, keys in hand, and the thought of stepping outside—of the air, the light, the possibility of seeing that sedan again—paralyzed her. Her husband found her weeping and drove her to a therapist that afternoon. Now, in the intake office, she sits with her hands folded in her lap, unable to explain the whole story from beginning to end. She says only, “I keep seeing his picture in my head. I can’t make it stop.” She is afraid of what it would mean to let her guard down completely, and she is equally afraid of spending whatever years she has left looking over her shoulder.
